definition: A series of statements which returns some value to a caller. It can be passed zero or more arguments which may be used in the execution of the body. In Python, defined with the def keyword.
A template for creating user-defined objects. Class definitions normally contain method definitions which operate on instances of the class. Supports inheritance, encapsulation, and polymorphism.
A function which is defined inside a class body. If called as an attribute of an instance of that class, the method will get the instance object as its first argument (usually called self).
connective_patterns: method takes self as first argument

definition: A named reference to an object stored in memory. In Python, variables are dynamically typed—the type is associated with the object, not the variable name. Assignment binds a name to an object.
A value passed to a function or method when calling it. Two kinds: keyword argument (preceded by an identifier, e.g. name=value) and positional argument (determined by position in the call).
A statement that exits a function and optionally passes back a value to the caller. If no return statement is executed, the function returns None. Multiple values can be returned as a tuple.

A function returning another function, usually applied as a function transformation using the @wrapper syntax. Common examples include @classmethod, @staticmethod, @property. The decorator syntax is syntactic sugar: @dec def f(): ... is equivalent to f = dec(f).

A function which returns a generator iterator. It looks like a normal function except that it contains yield expressions for producing a series of values usable in a for-loop or retrieved one at a time with next(). Generators are memory-efficient for large data streams.

A more generalized form of subroutines. Coroutines can be entered, exited, and resumed at many different points. In Python, implemented with the async def statement. Used for concurrent programming with the asyncio event loop.

A programming paradigm where operations can be initiated without waiting for their completion, allowing other operations to proceed concurrently. In Python, async def defines a coroutine function, and async for/async with provide asynchronous iteration and context management.

An expression used within coroutines that pauses execution until the awaitable object completes and returns its result. Can only be used inside an async def function. Yields control back to the event loop while waiting.

A subroutine function which is passed as an argument to be executed at some point in the future, typically when an event occurs or an asynchronous operation completes. Central to event-driven and asynchronous programming.

An object representing a stream of data. Repeated calls to its __next__() method return successive items. When no more data are available, StopIteration is raised. Required to have an __iter__() method returning itself, so every iterator is also iterable.

An event that disrupts the normal flow of a program's execution. In Python, exceptions are objects inheriting from BaseException. They are raised with raise and caught with try/except. Used for error handling and control flow signaling.
connective_patterns: exception propagates up the call stack

definition: Python's exception handling construct. The try block contains code that might raise exceptions; except blocks catch and handle specific exception types. Optional else block runs if no exception occurred; finally block always executes for cleanup.

The process by which Python code in one module is made available to Python code in another module. The import system searches for modules, creates module objects, and binds names in the importing namespace.

An object that serves as an organizational unit of Python code. Modules have a namespace containing arbitrary Python objects. Modules are loaded into Python by the process of importing. Each .py file is a module.

A Python module which can contain submodules or recursively subpackages. Technically, a package is a Python module with a __path__ attribute. Regular packages use __init__.py files; namespace packages span multiple directories.

A package or module that another package requires to function. Dependencies are declared in requirements.txt, setup.py, or pyproject.toml. Dependency management ensures compatible versions are installed together.

A technique where a function calls itself to solve a problem by breaking it into smaller subproblems of the same type. Requires a base case to terminate. Python has a default recursion limit of 1000 frames.

The process of repeatedly executing a block of code, typically over elements of a collection or until a condition is met. In Python, for loops iterate over iterables; while loops iterate based on conditions.

The region of a program where a name binding is valid. Python follows the LEGB rule: Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in. Variables in inner scopes can reference outer scopes but cannot assign to them without nonlocal or global declarations.

A function object that retains access to variables from its enclosing lexical scope even after the outer function has finished executing. In Python, a closure is created when a nested function references a free variable from an enclosing scope.

An OOP mechanism where a class (subclass) derives attributes and methods from another class (superclass). Python supports single and multiple inheritance. The Method Resolution Order (MRO) determines the order of method lookup.

The ability of different types to respond to the same interface or method call in type-specific ways. In Python, achieved through duck typing (if it quacks like a duck), method overriding, and protocol conformance.

The bundling of data and methods that operate on that data within a single unit (class), restricting direct access to some components. Python uses naming conventions (_private, __mangled) rather than strict access modifiers.

The process of hiding implementation details and showing only essential features. In Python, achieved through abstract base classes (ABC), protocols, and well-designed interfaces. Reduces complexity by exposing only relevant information.

A contract specifying a set of methods that a class must implement. Python does not have a formal interface keyword but uses abstract base classes (abc.ABC) and typing.Protocol for structural subtyping to define interfaces.

In Python typing, a Protocol (PEP 544) defines structural subtyping—a class conforms to a protocol if it has the required attributes and methods, regardless of explicit inheritance. Also refers to dunder protocols like __iter__, __len__.

The type of a Python object determines what kind of object it is. Every object has a type, accessible via type(obj) or obj.__class__. Python is dynamically typed (types checked at runtime) and supports type hints (PEP 484) for static analysis.
The process of converting an object into a format that can be stored or transmitted (e.g., JSON, pickle, msgpack) and later reconstructed. Deserialization is the reverse process.

Application Programming Interface: a set of defined rules and protocols that allow different software components to communicate. Includes function signatures, class interfaces, REST endpoints, and library public interfaces.
A specific URL path in a web API that accepts requests and returns responses. Each endpoint typically corresponds to a specific resource or operation (e.g., GET /users, POST /orders).
A mapping between a URL pattern and a handler function in a web framework. Routes determine which code handles which HTTP requests. In Flask: @app.route('/path'); in FastAPI: @app.get('/path').

A background process that runs continuously without direct user interaction, typically started at system boot. In Python, daemon threads are background threads that are automatically killed when the main thread exits.

An instance of a program in execution with its own memory space, file descriptors, and system resources. Processes are isolated from each other by the OS. Python's multiprocessing module creates separate processes to bypass the GIL.

A lightweight unit of execution within a process that shares memory space with other threads. In CPython, the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) limits true parallelism of threads for CPU-bound tasks, but threads remain useful for I/O-bound work.

The ability of a system to handle multiple tasks that can overlap in time. Concurrency does not require parallelism—tasks may interleave on a single core. Python offers threading (I/O-bound), multiprocessing (CPU-bound), and asyncio (cooperative).

A situation where two or more tasks wait indefinitely for each other to release resources or complete actions. For example, thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2, while thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1. Avoided by acquiring locks in a consistent order.

A flaw where the behavior of a program depends on the relative timing of events (e.g., thread scheduling). Occurs when multiple threads access shared data without proper synchronization, leading to unpredictable results.

Mutual exclusion lock: a synchronization primitive that ensures only one thread can access a critical section at a time. In Python, threading.Lock() provides a basic mutex. Must be released after acquisition to avoid deadlock.

A First-In-First-Out (FIFO) data structure where elements are added at the rear and removed from the front. Python provides queue.Queue (thread-safe), collections.deque, and asyncio.Queue for different concurrency models.

A Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) data structure where elements are pushed onto and popped from the top. Used for function call management (call stack), expression evaluation, backtracking algorithms, and undo operations.

Two meanings: (1) A tree-based data structure satisfying the heap property (parent >= children for max-heap). Used for priority queues. Python's heapq module implements a min-heap. (2) The region of memory for dynamic allocation.

A function that maps data of arbitrary size to fixed-size values. Used in dict/set for O(1) average lookup. In Python, objects must implement __hash__() to be usable as dict keys or set members. Mutable objects should not be hashable.

A storage layer that saves copies of frequently accessed data for faster retrieval. Can be in-memory (dict, functools.lru_cache), on-disk, or distributed (Redis, Memcached). Trade-off between speed and data freshness.

A data structure consisting of nodes (vertices) connected by edges. Can be directed or undirected, weighted or unweighted, cyclic or acyclic. Represented as adjacency lists, adjacency matrices, or edge lists.
A fundamental unit in a graph or tree data structure representing an entity. Contains data and connections (edges) to other nodes. Also called vertex in graph theory.

A connection between two nodes in a graph. Can be directed (one-way) or undirected (two-way), and may carry a weight or label. In a directed graph, an edge from A to B does not imply an edge from B to A.
connective_patterns: directed edge from A to B

definition: The process of visiting all nodes in a graph or tree data structure systematically. Common strategies: Breadth-First Search (BFS, level by level) and Depth-First Search (DFS, branch by branch).

Breadth-First Search: a graph traversal algorithm that visits all neighbors of a node before moving to the next level. Uses a queue. Guarantees shortest path in unweighted graphs. Time complexity O(V+E).

Depth-First Search: a graph traversal algorithm that explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking. Uses a stack (or recursion). Used for topological sort, cycle detection, connected components. Time complexity O(V+E).

A maximal subgraph of an undirected graph in which every pair of vertices is connected by a path. In directed graphs, strongly connected components require paths in both directions between every pair.

A linear ordering of vertices in a DAG such that for every directed edge (u,v), u comes before v. Used for dependency resolution, build systems, and task scheduling. Only possible for directed acyclic graphs.
Directed Acyclic Graph: a directed graph with no cycles. Fundamental structure for dependency graphs, task scheduling, version control (git), data pipelines, and neural network computation graphs.

A distributed version control system that tracks changes in source code. Uses a DAG of commits, where each commit is a snapshot of the repository. Supports branching, merging, rebasing, and distributed collaboration.
In git, a snapshot of the repository at a point in time. Each commit has a unique SHA-1 hash, a parent reference (forming a DAG), author info, timestamp, and a message describing the change.

In git, a lightweight movable pointer to a commit. Branches enable parallel development of features, bug fixes, and experiments. The default branch is typically main or master. Creating a branch is O(1) in git.

In git, the process of combining changes from two branches into one. Fast-forward merge moves the pointer; three-way merge creates a new merge commit. Conflicts arise when the same lines are changed differently in both branches.
